description:
Shaheen-e-Falak (شاہینِ فلک) – “Eagle of the Skies” 🦅🔥

Faisalabad team on Flame in Free Fall: using AI to predict how fire behaves in microgravity, a key astronaut safety risk. 

Lead: Kainat Rizwan, CEO KaiRiz Cyber Technologies, Senior Lecturer TMUC, PhD candidate (AI & Cybersecurity), 10+ published papers. 

We'll build an ML model on NASA combustion data plus an interactive dashboard. Seeking: Python/ML, web dev, data viz, video/storytelling. 

Beginners welcome!
summary: Flame in Freefall Atlas is an SI-powered, explainable web dashboard that turns decades of NASA microgravity combustion research into fire-safety answers for spacecraft, Moon habitats and spacesuits. Users choose a crew environment (ISS cabin, Moon habitat, exploration atmosphere or spacesuit, or custom oxygen, pressure and airflow) and the Atlas ranks 21 NASA investigations, including BASS-II, Saffire, ACME, SoFIE and FLEX, explaining every score. It maps where NASA has and hasn't tested, answers questions with quoted NASA findings, and includes a multi-sensor fire early-warning detector that fuses CO, CO₂ and smoke to catch fires before a smoke alarm, without false alarms from crew breathing. This matters because fire behaves differently without gravity. Earth flammability limits must be de-rated by at least 2.4% O₂ in orbit, and in spacecraft fires toxic gas, not heat, is the main danger. The Atlas also exposes critical gaps, such as no partial-gravity combustion data, to guide future Artemis-era research.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Without gravity there is no buoyancy, so flames become dim blue spheres fed only by diffusion, and materials can burn at lower oxygen levels than on Earth. NASA has studied this for 30 years (BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, ACME, Saffire, SoFIE), but the results are scattered across reports. Flame in Freefall Atlas makes them usable for the people designing Artemis-era habitats:

• Scenario ranking: enter oxygen, pressure, ventilation, gravity, material and hazard, or choose ISS cabin, Moon habitat, exploration atmosphere or spacesuit. Each of 21 NASA investigations gets a 0–100 score with a visible breakdown and plain-language reasons. An automatic safety brief flags conditions outside every tested envelope.

• Fire early-warning detector: learns the cabin's normal sensor baseline without labels, tracks each sensor with robust CUSUM change detection, and fuses CO, CO₂ and smoke by combustion physics. On an illustrative trace shaped to NASA's Saffire VI flight results, it alarms about 14 minutes before the smoke threshold, while a CO₂ rise from crew exercise does not trigger a false alarm. Users can upload their own sensor logs.

• Ask the Atlas: questions are answered with sentences quoted from NASA findings, each with its source. Nothing is invented.

• Test coverage map: oxygen vs pressure envelopes of NASA tests with crew environments overlaid, showing the evidence gap for Moon habitats and 100% oxygen spacesuits.

• Buoyancy simulator: drag gravity from orbit to the Moon, Mars and Earth and watch a flame change from a blue sphere into a yellow teardrop.

• Mission timeline, side-by-side comparison, evidence gaps, Earth applications, live NASA NTRS literature search, and CSV/JSON export of quantitative data points for predictive modelling.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Engineers, researchers and students can find the right evidence in seconds instead of searching dozens of reports. The Atlas also shows what we don't know yet: no partial-gravity combustion data, little testing at 30% or more oxygen at low pressure, and no coverage of pure-oxygen suits. Those gaps point future NASA experiments where they matter most. On Earth, the same multi-sensor approach can cut false alarms and speed up fire detection in homes, ships and data centres.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript only, with no frameworks or dependencies. It runs offline in any browser and is hosted on GitHub Pages. Source code: https://github.com/DrKainatRizwan/flame-in-freefall

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

We chose explainable AI on purpose: NASA's microgravity fire data is small and safety-critical, so every score and alarm is transparent and traceable to a NASA source. Values a source does not report are left blank, never guessed, and synthetic demo data is clearly labelled. The interface is built for non-experts as well as researchers, and it works on mobile. As future missions generate more sensor data, the detector can be upgraded to a trained deep-learning model.

SI DISCLOSURE

Code, text and the demo video were produced with Super Intelligence assistance (Claude, Anthropic). This is disclosed in the site footer, page metadata, README and a visible watermark on the video. All NASA data values were checked by the team against the cited sources.
